title: Placaeus: original rectitude a natural gift, propagated by generation; grace only as a free gift, not as Christ's favor to sinners
source_text: XXIX. Josue Placeus in Syntagmate Thesium Salmuriensium Disputatione de statu Adami ante lapsum, Thesi decima octava, dicit rectitudinem originalem primi hominis naturalibus donis annumerandam fuisse, quoniam nihil aliud fuit, quam congruentia cum lege naturae, & perfectio quae fuit simul cum natura creata, & quae per naturalem generationem propaganda erat, adeoque perfectio naturalis naturalibus hominis facultatibus respondens. Thesi vero vigesima sexta concedit justitiam Originalem fuisse quidem gratiam, hoc est, donum gratuitum ab eisdem tribus personis profectum, a quibus natura ipsa creata fuit: & gratiam non fuisse, quo sensu hoc nomen opponitur naturae, & significat effecta favoris divini quo Deus peccatores prosequitur in Christo.
pass_a_gloss: Josué de la Place in the Syntagma of the Saumur Theses, Disputation on the state of Adam before the fall, Thesis eighteen, says that the original rectitude of the first man was to be counted among natural gifts, since it was nothing else than congruence with the law of nature, and a perfection which was created together with nature, and which was to be propagated by natural generation, and so a natural perfection answering to the natural faculties of man. But in Thesis twenty-six he concedes that Original justice was indeed grace, that is, a gratuitous gift proceeding from the same three persons from whom nature itself was created: and that it was not grace in the sense in which this name is opposed to nature, and signifies the effects of divine favor by which God pursues sinners in Christ.
pass_b_english: Josué de la Place, in the Syntagma of Saumur Theses, disputation on the state of Adam before the fall, thesis 18, says that the first man's original rectitude should be counted among natural gifts. It was nothing other than agreement with the law of nature, a perfection created together with nature and meant to be handed on by natural generation, and so a natural perfection answering to man's natural faculties.

In thesis 26 he grants that original righteousness was indeed a grace, in the sense of a free gift coming from the same three persons who created nature itself. But it was not a grace in the sense in which the word is opposed to nature and means the effects of the divine favor with which God follows sinners in Christ.
